title: ‘Best day of my life’ – Antonelli reflects on Monza triumph
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has labelled his victory at the Italian Grand Prix “the best day of my life”, with the Mercedes driver hoping to add some more wins to his tally before the end of the season.

A planned engine change, and resultant penalties, meant that the 20-year-old was relegated to the back of the grid for his home race, but the pace of the W17 and the overtaking spots around Monza meant that he was always capable of limiting the damage.

What wasn’t expected was Antonelli charging from P19 to contend for the win, with the Italian getting stuck into multiple exhilarating battles with his team mate George Russell before crossing the line 3.857s clear.

It not only felt like a landmark result in his second campaign with Mercedes, but also helped to extend his advantage to 66 points in the Drivers’ Championship, so it’s no surprise that he is still savouring his performance ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix.

“The weekend itself was absolutely incredible,” Antonelli said in Madrid. “Definitely so far the best day of my life, and an incredible memory. I couldn’t wish for a better day.

“I didn’t fully realise [what I did] because I also didn’t have much time to do so. I think after this weekend I will have a bit more time to think about it. Of course, I want to do well this weekend as well.

“Looking back at that day, I think everything was incredible, and for sure the most memorable moment was when I crossed the line and then went on the podium. To see all the Tifosi, this massive crowd of people that was endless, was absolutely incredible.

“Hearing them singing the national anthem was also very, very special. It was fun coming back through the field, chasing, and then finally crossing the line was a big relief and very emotional.”

He went on to explain that while the race proved to him that “nothing’s impossible”, especially as his initial ambition was simply to recover to the podium, he’s now switched his focus to succeeding at the brand-new Madring.

Antonelli added: “I had goosebumps all the way. The next day I re-watched the podium and everything, and I still had goosebumps because obviously you dream of winning your home race. Doing it in that way and then seeing all the crowd cheering, it was absolutely special.

“The song at the end was the cherry on top of the cake. You know, singing that obviously super-famous song, and a really cool one. It is stuck in my head as well. Also within the team now, we’re all singing it. So hopefully we will have a reason to sing it this weekend as well.

“I wish [I had] a bit more time to realise and enjoy it, but now obviously we’re in Madrid and we’re ready to do our best, and we’ll try to repeat [it].”

title: The key challenges F1 drivers will tackle at the Madring
excerpt:
Having sampled the brand-new Madring in team simulators, Formula 1 drivers will finally get their first proper look when they take to the track in FP1 on Friday.

Throughout Thursday, ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix weekend, the talk was of how challenging this weekend is going to be. It goes without saying that a high-speed circuit surrounded by walls will punish mistakes, as was evident at the recent Formula 3 test.

But what about some of the more specific challenges presented by the new venue? Here are some that were highlighted by drivers today...

Curving braking areas will be tricky

Several drivers have noted how tricky some of the curving Madrid braking areas are, with the cars still turning while slowing down.

“You've got a lot of straight line braking,” said Kimi Antonelli. “But a lot of brakings where you're actually still turning.

"For example, Turn 17 is a corner where, when you hit the brake, you're still turning, and then you straighten the car. So it's very tricky track.”

“The walls are very close, so there's no margin for error,” said his Mercedes team mate George Russell. “But then you have other corners that are quite like Baku, where you're coming from a high speed into a slow braking zone, you're braking and turning at the same time.

“So locking tyres is going to be easy, and if you lock up, you'll be straight in the wall. I think it's going to be really challenging for us as drivers, very challenging. But very exciting at the same time, with zero margin for mistakes.”

'Insane' - What the F1 drivers make of the new Madring

Blind corners

Much like Jeddah, in several high-speed parts of the track the drivers have limited vision between the curving walls.

That obviously makes it tricky if an incident occurs up ahead, or if a car is travelling slowly due to an issue, or simply because it’s on an in-lap or out-lap.

“We have a lot of blind corners,” said Lando Norris. “A lot of the corners you cannot see around, so it's difficult to predict things. This just makes it always a bigger challenge inside the cockpit of a car – the fact you cannot see more than 50% of a corner at the end of one time.”

“Without stating the obvious, a lot of walls, a lot of high-speed corners, a lot of blind corners,” Alex Albon added. “[It] gives me vibes of Macau, but more for an F1 track."

Set-up will involve compromises

At every circuit they go to teams have to find the ideal aero compromise between performance gained on the straights and in the corners.

At the Madring it will be particularly complicated given the variety of turns, and the speed to be gained by riding kerbs.

“Driving-wise, you've got all kind of corners, you've got chicanes, fast corners, banked corners, medium speed,” Antonelli explains. “It's also complicated on the engineering side, because I think finding a set-up that is a good compromise for the whole lap is not going to be easy.

"You can find a set-up that helps you in the chicanes when you need to cut kerbs, or a set-up that helps you in the fast corners.

“But to find a set-up that is good over kerbs, good on change of direction, and good on fast corners, is going to be difficult, because whenever you do a set-up, there's always pros and cons. It helps in some ways, in some corners, but in others it might make your life a bit harder.”

Energy deployment has to keep up with corner speeds

It’s not just the chassis set-up that will be difficult for the teams. As grip ramps up over the course of the weekend, corners become faster, and that in turn has a direct influence on energy deployment – a lift in a fast corner has a big impact compared to staying flat.

In the same vein with low fuel and new soft tyres for Qualifying, as well as more rubber on the track after three practice sessions and support events, cornering speeds will increase for the cars down the order. Their power units will be operating in unfamiliar territory at the most critical point in the weekend.

Everything you need to know about the Madring

“There's a lot of corners on this track that will be between 90% and 100% throttle,” Albon said. “I think for the top teams it will be flat out, for the midfield teams and the back of the field teams, a bigger lift, which has a big effect on deployment.

“So without going too technical, if you do a corner flat or not massively changes the way the deployment works. You don't want to go into Qualifying and suddenly all these corners start to become flat, and your deployment starts to move around a lot.”

Overtaking will be difficult on Sunday

Sim running has indicated that overtaking won’t be easy in the race, and Williams' Albon has an intriguing take on why.

“You've got a lot of combined corners, which just thinking of overtaking on Sunday, it feels like it's quite easy to defend,” he said. “You just put the car in the middle of the track, and you're not going to get a car that's going to go past you. So that just means that it will be more of a deployment overtake than a braking overtake.”

The difficulty in overtaking will in turn put a sharp focus on having a fast car over one lap, something that has already caught the attention of Charles Leclerc.

“I think it's the kind of weekend where you want to focus more on the qualifying pace than on the race pace,” said the Ferrari driver. “Because come Sunday, I feel like it's going to be difficult – apart from the start – to kind of gain positions.

“So for sure, our priority will be to try and maximise the practices in order to make sure that in Q3 we end up with the right car, and with a good lap. So yeah, the priority will be shifted a little bit more towards Qualifying.

“I still think the race can be interesting with the strategy, but maybe with the overtaking a bit less than other tracks.”

The perfect lap will be hard to nail

The sheer number of corners to get right and the need in 2026 to optimise battery usage mean that it won’t be easy to nail the perfect lap in Qualifying.

There’s also the challenge of tyre management – you have to have the fronts up to temperature for the corners at the start of the lap, while avoiding rear overheating later on. And inevitably there will be traffic.

“It's going to be a very interesting track to drive,” said Liam Lawson. “Very technical, obviously, I think just quite challenging for us. And through the weekend, trying to put laps together, I think it's one of those tracks that you're not going to feel like you've nailed a lap.

“Honestly, half the time there are going to be one or two mistakes in a lap – probably all the time. It's quite difficult.”

Gabriel Bortoleto added: “I think basically all the corners are very challenging. But probably T5 and T6 are going to be very challenging, with lots of kerb usage there, and then going a bit uphill and then downhill, and then having some high-speed corners just after.

“I think that’s the typical type of track that you finish a lap and you can really feel your breathing, because it’s very mentally exhausting through the lap. And to nail a perfect lap is also difficult – but when you do it, it’s very, very promising.”

title: How Verstappen and Lawson rate Red Bull's chances in Madrid
excerpt:
Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson have rated Red Bull's chances at this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, with the Madring set to host its inaugural Formula 1 event.

The high-speed street circuit promises to offer drivers and teams a new challenge that could open the door for an unexpected result.

Red Bull and Verstappen have yet to register a win this season, with the Dutchman suggesting that the perils of a street circuit, along with the unknown of a new venue, could potentially give him his best chance yet.

"I think the practice sessions are crucial, and hopefully we just get a good feeling with the car. I think if you have a good feeling with the car, you’re actually a bit more competitive, and hopefully that will put us into a place where we can fight again around a podium," he said.

"I always try my best to try and win a race, at least this year, but for sure it’s not going to be easy to win a race. But we’ll see. Maybe, first race here, we can have a bit of chaos. You need to luck in maybe a little bit, but we keep trying.

"It probably is a car killer [circuit] from what I’ve seen so far. You just need to try and stay out of the wall, try and get the best possible feeling in the car. When you are confident in the car on a street circuit, it helps a lot.

"It’s difficult to say at the moment how everything is going to go. And, I mean, driver track or not, you still need a good car. That’s the most important thing."

Lawson, meanwhile, will continue to stand in for the injured Isack Hadjar having already raced for Red Bull in Zandvoort and Monza.

The New Zealander missed out on points last weekend in Italy but believes he is adapting further to Red Bull's 2026 challenger, which will be even more crucial at a new venue.

"This track is quite different to what we've been racing on. It's obviously new for all of us so it's going to take some time to learn," he said.

"For us as drivers, the teams as well with the car, I'm sure it's going to be challenging but the more time I spend in the car the more I'm going to naturally get a bit more comfortable.

Lawson added: "It's not my car and obviously in your own car you have many things that are very suited for you, and that's not something I can do in a couple of races with this car. More time I spend in it, more comfortable I get."

title: ‘My team mate has done a better job than me’ – Russell
excerpt:
George Russell believes that over the course of the 2026 season so far, his Mercedes team mate Kimi Antonelli “has done a better job” and “deserves to be leading” the Drivers’ Championship, but he is not giving up on the title fight quite yet.

After a dominant opening round, Russell began to struggle as Antonelli went on a remarkable run of five Grand Prix victories, and while Ferrari and McLaren have taken wins of their own, the Italian driver has steadily eked out a 66-point lead.

It puts him in a strong position to become the youngest-ever champion, leaving Russell to admit that he’s under no illusions about the likelihood of overhauling his deficit over the remaining rounds.

He explained: “I'm not trying to be delusional, the reality is my team mate has done a better job than me this year. Had some bad luck but he deserves to be leading and right now he deserves to be in the position he is.

“From my side, I'm just going race by race, going to try and win as many as possible. If I want to win this championship I'm going to need some luck and that's where we are. I'm being quite realistic about the position we're in.”

The comments come after Antonelli stormed from a P19 start to win the Italian Grand Prix, during which he repeatedly went wheel-to-wheel with his team mate before demoting Russell to P2.

Asked how he has dealt with the loss, the Briton replied: “[I’ve had] good practice of processing stuff this year. I'm feeling good, taken positives away from every weekend. I would have loved to have won the race in Monza, loved to have continued that fight with Kimi.

“The fact is, he's just doing an amazing job right now and you have to give him credit for that. I've been making some good improvements and still want to keep on that journey to take the fight back to him. That's the mentality I have right now.”

He can put that into action this weekend, with the Madring set to host its inaugural Spanish Grand Prix. Being a brand-new circuit with plenty of unknowns, it could shake up the pecking order and create a chance for Russell to return to the top step.

“The level of everyone in F1 is exceptionally high,” he said. “It’s going to be a circuit where you need confidence.

“Very challenging, lots of high speed corners, aggressive kerbs. Going to be an experience for sure. Just try and keep out of the wall and build up to it.

“Every race is an opportunity. This circuit is among the most risky circuits of the season. You want to put everything on the line and go for pole and victory but how I approach this race, it's just going about business as usual.”

title: 'Insane' – What the F1 drivers make of the new Madring
excerpt:
Formula 1 drivers will once again get to experience the thrill of racing at a new circuit at this weekend’s Spanish Grand Prix, where excitement for the unknown has already spread through the paddock at the Madring.

Spain’s capital city is welcoming F1 back for the first time in 45 years with a purpose-built track that combines public roads with permanent sections. Its high speeds, twisty layout and unique banked corner – suitably named La Monumental – have already generated plenty of discussion about what to expect.

While the action won’t begin until Free Practice 1 at 1330 local time on Friday, September 11, many have already used the simulator to get a feel for the venue, and early reactions bode well for the competitive sessions.

Someone who’s especially looking forward to the round is Madrid-born Carlos Sainz, who is not only about to experience his first true home race, but also serves as a circuit ambassador.

The Spaniard was the first on the grid to complete a lap of the Madring, albeit in a road car when it was still incomplete. At the time, he called it “honestly impressive” and admitted that he “didn’t expect it to be so flowing, so wide” – comments which he added to upon his return to the city.

“I’m for sure going to enjoy this a lot,” he told the media on Thursday. “It’s going to be busy, but also emotional. I’m going to try and enjoy it as much as possible. It looks like the track has a character that is charismatic, with a lot of different types of corners.”

His countryman Fernando Alonso has 25 years of racing in Spain as an F1 driver under his belt, but that doesn’t mean that this weekend will be any less remarkable for him. Instead, it’s the opposite, as he was keen to embrace the chance to compete twice in the nation in the same season, having already ticked off the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix.

“It's going to be a very nice weekend,” Alonso said. “We have this privilege to race two times in Spain this year, and for the very first time in Madrid. It is special. Also a new track, so it adds this challenge for everyone to learn the track as quick as possible in Free Practice. For me, it’s double special being in Spain.

“Madrid is one of the best cities in the world so to have a Grand Prix and to welcome F1 here is incredible. I think for any racing driver, to win in Madrid will mean a lot.

“It’s very technical, lots of kerb riding and a couple of high-speed sections where you need to get very close to the walls, which is very attractive and very high adrenaline for a driver – close to Jeddah.”

Alpine’s Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto seemed similarly enthusiastic about the Madring after their strong outing in Monza, which saw the Frenchman clinch a shock pole position before the pair delivered a double points finish.

“The track itself on the simulator looked insane,” Gasly raved. “To drive it was very fun – lots of technical and twisty corners. From everything I’ve heard, it’s definitely something very unique. So, big challenge, but I’m excited for this type of weekend where everything is brand new for everyone.

“I think the challenge driving-wise should not be underestimated, because it’s 15 corners, and they’re absolutely crazy – with undulation, going up and down, banking, 90-degree corners, 180-degree corners, low speed, high speed – you name it, you’ve got a bit of everything.

Everything you need to know about the Madring

“It’s exciting. As a driver, it feels like you’re going to have many opportunities around the lap to actually make these small gains everywhere. I think the track layout is something I’ve never seen before. I’m sure we’re going to have huge adrenaline in the car.”

Colapinto, who lived in Madrid for a time, added: “I’m really excited to be back here in Spain. Madrid does feel like the closest to home, I think especially because of my previous experiences and how I started in Europe – I started here in Madrid.

“To be racing here in F1 is a dream come true. I think it’s very good for the sport as well to have another big city like Madrid being back on the calendar, putting a very exciting track [together]. It looks like a very good one to drive. It’s going to be cool.”

Cadillac driver Sergio Perez labelled it “a proper track”, while Ollie Bearman admitted that “new tracks are always incredibly fun for us” – possibly because as any incidents create more openings for midfield teams like Haas to score.

The frontrunners seem to be anticipating an interesting round too, with Mercedes’ George Russell targeting his first win since Round 8 in Austria.

“It seems a wild track to be fair,” he admitted. “It's mental but excited to experience it. Going to be a real challenge and I think Qualifying is going to be important.

“The level of everyone in F1 is exceptionally high. It’s going to be a circuit where you need confidence. Very challenging, lots of high speed corners, aggressive kerbs. Going to be an experience for sure. Just try and keep out of the wall and build up to it.”

title: Leclerc accepts blame in Hamilton Monza incident
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc admitted ahead of this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix that "it's pretty clear that I could have done a better job" following his on-track moment with Ferrari team mate Lewis Hamilton in Monza.

The Ferrari drivers went side-by-side through the opening chicane last weekend, with Hamilton finding himself in the gravel and dropping positions.

It was an incident which put a strain on Hamilton and Leclerc's relationship in the immediate aftermath, before the former stated on Thursday's media day in Madrid that the pair have "got a good racing relationship".

Leclerc confirmed the pair had spoken in the aftermath of the incident to clear the air, with the Monegasque driver admitting he was primarily at fault.

"Having the Turn 2 incident is not something we ever want to see again," he said. "And for that, reviewing the images, it’s pretty clear that I could have done a better job just slowing down the car and not putting Lewis then in a difficult situation.

"So this is something I can learn from, for sure, but we’ve already spoken with Lewis.

"I think what was very important was to speak, first of all. It's been quite a few years now that I’m in Ferrari — and I kind of know how it feels when everything around Ferrari is kind of on fire.

"And if you don’t speak between Lewis and I, then you can get caught up with this noise that there is around the team.

"It’s not that there are no reasons for that noise, but I think the intensity of the noise is a bit too crazy. When you look at Monza, there’s been friction between other team mates and we barely talk about it.

"But when it’s about Ferrari, it takes proportions that are not normal. But we spoke with Lewis. We’ve always had a great relationship.

"I have a lot of respect for Lewis, and I told him that in Turn 2 I didn’t behave the way I should have, and the way a team mate should."

Leclerc's race in Monza came to an end on just the second lap after suffering a heavy crash at the final corner, which brought out the red flag.

Although Leclerc was medically cleared, the Ferrari driver admits that he did suffer in the immediate aftermath of the crash, but that he will be fully fit for the new challenge of the Madring this weekend.

"I will be 100% fine. I mean, it was only right after the crash that it was just a little bit strange and I felt a little bit dizzy," he said.

"But very quickly, from Monday afternoon, I felt better. I had quite a few treatments for the neck, because that’s where most of the shock went, and I’m feeling good now.

"So I’m ready for this weekend. I did quite a lot of checks, and all checks were fully fine. So no worries for this weekend."

title: Hamilton opens up on ‘racing relationship’ with Leclerc
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has asserted that he shares “a good racing relationship” with Charles Leclerc after they came close to a disastrous collision at the beginning of the Italian Grand Prix, with the Briton praising Ferrari’s communication in the aftermath.

The pair started on the second row for the team’s home race at Monza, but any chance of a podium quickly disappeared as they went side-by-side at Turn 2 and Hamilton took to the gravel, subsequently tumbling down the order before Leclerc crashed not long after.

As he called on Ferrari to “change things” in terms of their approach to the drivers battling one another so they don’t end up “in jeopardy” again, Team Principal Fred Vasseur hinted that a discussion around rules of engagement was required.

Hamilton ultimately recovered to P6 and any tension around the incident seems to have been left in the past, with the focus quickly shifting to this weekend’s Spanish Grand Prix at the brand-new Madring.

Reflecting on his bond with Leclerc, the 41-year-old said: “I think we've got a good racing relationship. I think the fact [is] that we are grown ups and are able to communicate with each other, which we have.

“I'm really happy that he's really healthy and he's back here this weekend because we need him in the fight to challenge Mercedes together. There is all this discussion about communication and execution and stuff, but the communication between John [Elkann, Executive Chairman] and Benedetto [Vigna, Chief Executive Officer] and Fred, and his drivers, are really great.

“We all sit down and talk afterwards, squash it and move on so nothing lingers. We're just looking forward to how we can work better together.”

The frustrating result at Monza sam Hamilton drop to 76 points behind standings leader Kimi Antonelli – roughly the equivalent of three Grand Prix victories.

But with 10 rounds remaining, there is still hope in the Ferrari camp that they can continue to take the fight to Mercedes and stay in contention for the championship, with Hamilton’s sights set on a record-breaking eighth drivers’ title.

“I'm still a believer that Ferrari has absolutely everything we need to win,” he concluded. “It takes everything coming together, naturally, to be able to achieve what we're trying to achieve.

“It's also difficult when you're fighting against the team just ahead on performance. I think we just have to continue. We've built a really good foundation with this first part of the year and we just have to continue to build on it. The team has worked incredibly hard to bring upgrades weekend in and weekend out.

“We've just obviously taken a step with the engine, which is a real positive. I think it's really important to just acknowledge that. I trust in everything that we're doing, the steps we're taking. Trusting Fred, and I really believe that we will get to where we're going. Whether it's next week, several weeks’ time or next year, we'll just keep pushing.”

title: Formula 1's Spanish football connections
excerpt:
Formula 1 heads to Madrid this weekend, with the all-new Madring preparing to host the Spanish Grand Prix as the sport returns to the capital for the first time in 45 years.

It also arrives at quite the moment for Spanish football. Both their women’s and men’s national teams are World Champions, while Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid are both getting involved in F1's newest race. Add in Carlos Sainz and Fernando Alonso's love of the beautiful game, and there are plenty of connections between the two sports.

Ahead of the first Grand Prix at the Madring, let's take a look at some of the biggest links between Formula 1 and Spanish football...

Madridistas in the paddock

When it comes to choosing between the two sides of Madrid, there is little debate for Sainz and Alonso, with both firmly in the Real Madrid camp.

The Spanish pair have supported Los Blancos through their fathers' influence. Indeed, before becoming a two-time World Rally Champion and four-time Dakar Rally winner, Sainz Sr even had trials with Real Madrid as a teenager.

Both F1 drivers have been regular visitors to the club and have often brought their support into the paddock by arriving at races wearing Real Madrid shirts.

Alonso's connection with the club went one step further in 2017, when the two-time F1 World Champion was made an official honorary member of Real Madrid, the highest distinction the club can award. Sainz Sr later received the same honour in 2021.

For Sainz Jr, Real Madrid will now be even closer when he takes part in his first Grand Prix in his home city. The Williams driver was born and raised in Madrid and has been closely involved with the new event as a Madring ambassador, becoming the first driver to complete a lap of the finished 5.4km circuit earlier this year.

Real Madrid's new racing neighbours

Sainz and Alonso won't be the only Real Madrid representation around the Madring this weekend. Ahead of the inaugural race, Real Madrid became an official Local Event Supporter of the Spanish Grand Prix, and the location of their famous training complex makes the partnership particularly fitting.

Real Madrid City and the northern section of Madring are neighbours in Valdebebas, with just 200 metres separating the circuit's northern entrance and the main gate of the club's training base. Selected club facilities will be incorporated into Grand Prix operations, while Real Madrid will also have a presence within hospitality areas across the weekend.

It means F1 cars will be racing only a short distance away from the training ground used by some of the biggest names in world football.

There is even a newly crowned World Champion among them. Marc Cucurella joined Real Madrid this summer after Spain's triumph at the 2026 World Cup, having played every minute of the tournament for La Roja.

Atletico get in on the action

The Madrid football connection doesn't stop with Real. Atletico Madrid have also joined forces with the Spanish Grand Prix, agreeing a five-year partnership to become a Local Event Supporter of the race.

Their involvement stretches beyond Madring itself, with the Riyadh Air Metropolitano set to become another hub for fans across the weekend. The stadium will host fan experiences and hospitality, as well as the main concert connected to the Grand Prix, while shuttle services will help transport fans towards the circuit.

How the new Madring circuit looks ahead of its inaugural Grand Prix

Atletico will also have their own presence at Madring, bringing another of the capital's biggest sporting names into F1's newest race.

The club also arrive into the weekend with plenty to celebrate, having had several players involved in Spain's World Cup-winning squad earlier this summer. According to the club, it was the largest number of players supplied by one team to a World Cup final since 1934.

Spain on top of the world

One member of the squad who lifted the World Cup earlier this summer has already made his way into the F1 paddock. Ferran Torres was a guest of Audi at Monza last weekend, where he got a closer look at the Audi R26 alongside Gabriel Bortoleto and race engineer Jose Manuel Lopez.

Torres was joined by a host of other footballing names across the Italian Grand Prix weekend, including Sandro Tonali, Curtis Jones, Serge Gnabry and Cesc Fabregas.

With Spain still celebrating their latest World Cup success, the crossover between the country's two sporting passions is set to continue as Formula 1 arrives in Madrid.

When El Clasico came to F1

Real Madrid and Barcelona have contested some fierce battles over the years, but in 2020 their rivalry found an unusual new setting: a Formula 1 grid.

With racing put on hold during the Covid-19 pandemic, F1 launched a series of Virtual Grands Prix featuring current drivers alongside stars from elsewhere in sport and entertainment.

For the Virtual Spanish Grand Prix, Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois lined up for Alfa Romeo while Barcelona midfielder Arthur Melo represented Haas.

And they weren't the only footballers swapping boots for a steering wheel. Then-Manchester City and Argentina striker Sergio Aguero joined Alex Albon at Red Bull, while F1 drivers including Charles Leclerc, Lando Norris and George Russell also competed.

The race took place around a virtual Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya, giving football fans a rather different version of an El Clasico battle.

Football fever in the F1 paddock

Football stars getting close to F1 machinery is certainly nothing new, and previous Spanish Grands Prix have attracted plenty of familiar faces from the game. The 2025 race in Barcelona was particularly football-heavy, with the England men's national team among those visiting the paddock on Sunday.

Real Madrid star Jude Bellingham was spotted alongside England team mate Bukayo Saka, while former Real Madrid and Brazil defender Roberto Carlos also made his way onto the grid.

Meanwhile, Robert Lewandowski was given one of the most important jobs of the weekend, waving the chequered flag as the cars crossed the line.

A year later, football was everywhere once again as the 2026 Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix coincided with the opening weekend of the World Cup.

Drivers tried their luck with a football goal inside the paddock, Pierre Gasly and Isack Hadjar took to a local pitch for a kickabout, and Racing Bulls transformed themselves into 'VCARB FC' with a football-inspired crest and special livery.

There have also been plenty of Spanish World Cup winners making appearances at F1 races over the years. Sergio Busquets, part of the side that lifted Spain's first men's World Cup in 2010, has visited several Grands Prix, including the Barcelona-Catalunya race earlier this season.

Now the crossover moves to Madrid

The Madring's 22 corners will provide a completely new challenge when cars hit the circuit for the first time this weekend, 45 years after F1 last raced in the Spanish capital at Jarama.

With one of the world's biggest football clubs training just metres away, another turning its stadium into part of the Grand Prix weekend, and Spain still celebrating World Cup glory, there should be no shortage of football fever when Formula 1 arrives in Madrid.

title: What Gasly’s Monza pole brings to Alpine ahead of Madrid
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly believes his Monza pole position "brings belief and motivation" to Alpine as the team look for another strong result this weekend at the Spanish Grand Prix.

Gasly's maiden Formula 1 pole position last weekend in Italy was one of the shocks of the season, and signified a remarkable turnaround for the Enstone-based team that spent much of 2025 towards the back of the grid.

Speaking on Thursday's media day ahead of the inaugural race at the Madring, Gasly believes the performance has given the entire team an extra boost which will keep them pushing towards the front.

"It meant a lot to all the team, because it’s not like we’ve had easy weekends, especially coming from last year into 2026," he said. "We put a lot of effort into this year’s car, and to actually get the reward from all that hard work from everyone was incredible.

"The smiles I could see on the faces in the garage, all the people at the factory – everyone was buzzing. I’m very pleased for all of them that we were able to do it.

"It just brings that extra confidence and boost of motivation that if we actually get everything right, this type of result — which seems unachievable — is actually possible. I think it definitely brings belief and motivation to try to do even better and repeat this type of performance.

"I told the guys it’s been 17 years since there was a pole for Enstone, and I’m not waiting another 17 years until we do another one. So it’s a great boost of motivation, and hopefully we can repeat that in the near future."

Drivers and teams will face a different test this weekend at the Madring, which features high-speed, banked corners around a circuit that is a new venue for all.

Gasly added "it’s going to be a proper racing track", and that "I have no idea about the racing yet, but driving-wise in the simulator it was incredible, so I’m excited to see what it’s like in real life."

Ahead of this weekend, the Frenchman also spent time with footballing legend Zinedine Zidane as the pair filmed a project together, with Gasly stating he was given some advice in the wake of Alpine's Monza success.

"I’m a big fan of Zizou, so it’s always nice. He’s such a nice guy, and it’s always great to actually have access to him," he said.

"He’s now the coach of our national team, so you know how much I love football. I was asking questions and trying to get a few bits of information on what’s coming."

title: Liam Lawson explains Madring 'mistakes' that will lead to F1 drivers 'in a wall'
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has explained how a simple mistake at the Madring will have F1 drivers "thrown straight at the wall" at the new Spanish GP venue.

The new 22-turn semi-street, semi-permanent circuit will host its first grand prix this weekend, with drivers anticipating a tricky challenge given the narrow nature of the track, with multiple blindspots around some of the corners.

It has been compared to the Jeddah Corniche Circuit in Saudi Arabia, where, in Sector 1, especially, the fast, flowing curves are blind with the walls, whilst in Sectors 2 and 3, the straights are curved, with walls partially blocking vision for the drivers.

One particular challenge which awaits is at Turns 5 and 6, at the end of the first straight mode activation zone, with drivers having to brake in a curved line to navigate the fast left-right-left flicks to head off up the hill to the tight Turn 8.

Lawson, who is still at Red Bull in place of the injured Isack Hadjar, explained that he watched videos from the recent F3 two-day test and how those drivers navigated the section at the "sketchy" circuit - and how mistakes from F1 drivers will have them "in the wall."

"It's going to be a very interesting track to drive; it is very technical, obviously. I think just quite challenging for us, and through the weekend, trying to put laps together," Lawson told media, including RacingNews365.

"I think it's one of those tracks that you're not going to feel like you've nailed a lap. Honestly, half the time it's going to be one or two mistakes a lap, probably all the time. It's quite difficult.

"Monaco was one where we could push flat out, and actually have no limitations. So I would say it's not like it's going to be like that, but I think it definitely is somewhere that is somewhere, more than Monza, where you can probably make a bit of a difference.

"I just think it's going to be very challenging for us to put a lap together to feel like you've nailed everything. If you do, it's probably going to make quite a big difference.

"But it's pretty sketchy in places, to be honest. It is very easy to get it wrong. It's not somewhere I feel like has a lot of flow. It's very technical, and it's hard to put it together, but it might be exciting enough for one car.

"The way these sort of street circuits are built, the walls, a lot of them just follow where the track goes, and they're just very blind in a lot of places, so in a lot of these faster-flowing corners where you have something behind it but you can't see it, and Jeddah obviously has more of that than this place, but it's similar in that way, I would say."

Turning to the challenge of the left-right-left chicane of Turns 5 and 6, Lawson explained how the car could be "thrown straight into the wall."

"The thing is, if you take too much of the first kerb, it'll bounce you across the second kerb, which will then just bounce you over the wall, so trying to be accurate through a section like that's quite tough," Lawson said.

"I've seen a lot of videos of F3 cars just smashing both the kerbs and getting away with it, not getting away with it. It's definitely a tricky part of the track. The braking zone is obviously not straight as well, so trying not to lock up and push that braking zone is going to be pretty tough, and then it also depends on your energy management- how much you're using.

"Because I think on tracks like this, when it's changing lap to lap, you approach at different speeds, and that can make it quite difficult to push a section like that.

"I mean, you do have the option to just bail and go straight, at least, but it's simply somewhere that if you take too much kerb, it'll just throw you straight into the left wall."

title: Audi launch appeal over Italian GP stewards' decision
excerpt:
Audi F1 team has confirmed it has indeed appealed the decision not to punish Yuki Tsunoda at the Italian Grand Prix last weekend.

At Monza, the Japanese driver avoided being penalised for a start infringement and went on to finish P10, picking up his first point of the campaign on just his second outing in place of Liam Lawson at Racing Bulls.

Specifically, Tsunoda was at an unusual angle in his starting box, having initially lined up on the wrong side of the grid following the Charles Leclerc-induced red flag stoppage.

Despite the 26-year-old being correctly in place, albeit in a strange way, the race director, Rui Marques, opted for a second formation lap, as they were not comfortable with Tsunoda starting with his car facing the pit wall so directly.

If a driver is deemed the cause of an extra formation lap, under Article B5.9.4 of the FIA sporting regulations, they must be moved to the pit lane.

However, given that Tsunoda was in his grid slot, even if unconventionally, the stewards determined that it was the race director, not the driver, who instigated the extra formation lap and that he was right to have taken the restart as normal.

Following that decision, Audi lodged its intention to appeal the verdict on the grounds that Tsunoda had been the original cause of the extra formation lap and that, therefore, his VCARB 03 should have been moved to the pit lane, which almost certainly would have meant a finish outside the top 10.

That started a 96-hour clock for the German team to actually file its appeal, which has now been confirmed in a statement: "Following the Italian Grand Prix, the team raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4, which requires a driver who causes an extra formation lap to enter the pit lane and resume the race from there.

"We can confirm that an appeal has been submitted within the 96-hour window mandated by the regulations. As the matter is now subject to the FIA appeal process, we will not comment further at this stage."

With Gabriel Bortoleto finishing P11 at the Temple of Speed, Audi stands to gain a championship point if the stewards' ruling is overturned.

title: Kimi Antonelli 'phone exploded' after best day of his life
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has joked that his 'phone exploded' following his stunning victory in Sunday's Italian Grand Prix.

Antonelli produced one of the greatest drives in F1 history by winning the race at Monza from 19th on the grid, beating team-mate George Russell, who had started from second.

The win means Antonelli has opened up a 66-point cushion over Russell in the drivers' standings with nine or 10 races remaining, depending on the situation in the Middle East and whether the season-closing events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will be replaced by a final grand prix in Europe.

Antonelli's triumph even resulted in Ferrari's passionate fans, the tifosi, chanting his name as he stood on the podium as the 20-year-old became the first Italian driver to win on home soil in 60 years.

Asked about the messages he received following his success, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, ahead of this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix at the new Madring street circuit, Antonelli said: "I received a lot.

"On WhatsApp, when I went into the app after the race, I got so many messages that the app crashed. So I went into the app and got out without even touching the phone because it exploded.

"But I received a lot of nice messages from Jannik [Sinner], [Marco] Bezzechi, Vale [Valentino Rossi], from literally everyone, so it was super nice to see so much support, so much enthusiasm, so much excitement. That was very, very cool.

"It's really hard to pick a message that stood out compared to all the others. All of them were super, super, super nice."

Antonelli reveals what brought him down to earth after Monza madness

Antonelli described what unfolded on Sunday as 'the best day of his life', one he will "remember forever".

The day after, rather than relaxing and basking in the glow of his win, Antonelli's enthusiasm for everything four wheels continued as he opted to go karting, allowing him to put the previous day in context.

"It is sometimes tough to stay calm or not to get too overexcited," said Antonelli. "Monza, that day overall was very exciting. But, for example, going karting on Monday helped me to go back to earth.

"It was a good fun day with with the team, a way to remind myself where I came from, the journey that I've done. So it was a good way to, first of all, have fun, to train, and then also to go back to earth."

title: Charles Leclerc provides health update after 'the shock' of major Monza smash
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has revealed it was "the shock" of his crash in Sunday's Italian Grand Prix that caused him the most consternation rather than suffering any physical issues that could have prevented him from competing in this Sunday's race in Madrid.

Leclerc suffered a 60g impact into a tyre wall after losing his Ferrari through Parabolica, destroying his SF-26. The Monégasque driver was clearly in distress as he sat on the grass after extracting himself from his car and whilst he waited for medical attention.

Leclerc revealed after the incident to suffering with an issue with his vision, albeit one that quickly rectified itself.

Asked whether there were any issues in the days that followed that may have prevented him from not driving this weekend at F1's newest circuit, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, Leclerc said: "No, not to that extent.

"I felt the tightness and a bit of pain in the neck on Monday, but in terms of vision, it was very short [the problem].

"Right after I got out of the car, one eye was, I don't know, maybe not working properly, but then it was fully fine after a few seconds, so I was not too worried.

"I knew it was a big shunt, and obviously that's never a good thing for the body, but straight away I could see quite nicely."

As to the medical checks that followed and whether they revealed anything, Leclerc added: "It [the crash] was quite a big one.

"Probably from the outside it looked like a big one as well, but it also felt like a big one. Sometimes it can look quite big from the outside, but from [inside] the car it's fine.

"But getting out, I wasn't feeling so well. Actually, it was just the shock. I did quite a lot of checks and had quite a lot of treatments in the first two days, mostly for the neck because I felt a little bit tight, which I guess is normal. But now I'm fine.

"All the checks I did were fine."

title: Max Verstappen explains why Red Bull has not cured long-standing problem
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has explained why Red Bull has been unable to fix a particular problem that has plagued the team for years.

Max Verstappen has addressed Red Bull's difficulties with bumps and kerbs, and why the Milton Keynes-based squad has struggled to remedy the issue across generations of F1.

It was a problem that saw the Dutchman and his team flounder at street circuits in recent years, where bumps and kerbs are prevalent, and that Achilles' heel has not gone away, despite this season ushering in a new era of F1 regulations.

Last weekend at Monza, the four-time F1 drivers' champion complained about the ride of his RB22, specifically its rear axle, especially over the bumps and kerbs of the Temple of Speed.

And with the championship venturing to the Madring for the first time this weekend, it promises to be another round where the six-time constructors' champions must face up to one of the team's oldest weaknesses.

"It's a known problem for us for a long time, so it's something that we are trying to figure out, trying to fix, trying to be better at," Verstappen told media, including RacingNews365.

"But we know that kerbs and bumps are not the best thing for our car."

'The answer is not very clear'

Because F1 teams all develop their own cars in a vacuum to the predetermined rulebook, it is commonplace for a certain team's car to retain particular characteristics, or a DNA, across regulation cycles.

"Yeah, for sure, some things carried over from the previous cars," the 71-time grand prix winner added.

"I was complaining about the ride and the kerbs before, and I'm still complaining about it. So, for sure, there are things that we are looking into to try and fix, but unfortunately, the answer is not very clear or straightforward because otherwise, of course, we would have fixed those things.

"F1 can sometimes be very complicated, and it cannot be easy to pinpoint one exact problem because it might be a few things that come together to create a problem, and you need to figure out all those details on the car to try to be better at a certain aspect."

title: Lewis Hamilton reveals Charles Leclerc talks after Monza tension
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has revealed how he and Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc "squashed" any lingering bad blood between the two after talks over their Italian GP tension.

At Turns 1 and 2 at Monza, Hamilton attempted to move up the inside of Leclerc, who then pushed the sister car into the gravel and down the order.

Post-race, Hamilton said there were "no rules here" regarding the so-called rules of engagement that he had against Nico Rosberg at Mercedes and that there was "no we" involved in the incident, as he felt he was ahead at the Turn 2 apex, and so had the right to position.

The seven-time champion has indicated his desire to be given preferential treatment at the team in the title race fight, as he was 59 points behind Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli prior to Monza, although this has now slipped to 76 - over three grands prix worth - following the Monza race.

Detailing talks which had taken place throughout the turnaround from Monza to Madrid, Hamilton revealed that he and Leclerc had sat face-to-face to clear the air, and that any lingering discontent had been "squashed."

"It's been really positive. I spoke to Fred on Monday, and we just had a clearing out discussion. Naturally, we can always have different opinions, but at the end of the day, we come together, and we find a way forward.

"That's the positives of where we've got to over the past 15 months or whatever it is. We've got to a place where we have really great communication internally, and the same with me and Charles.

I think if you just look at this, the history of this sport, this happened before, so it's no biggie.

When then asked about wanting rules of engagement and if it was discussed, Hamilton was firm that "it was not" and added that "I'm sure at some stage we'll discuss how we can be better, but we've not had a lot of time to turn around. You can't change things in two days.

"It is not something we can change into this weekend. There's a huge amount of moving parts. There are a lot of people. There's a culture that's been here for a long, long time, and moving big pieces is not so easy. And so we just take it one step at a time, and it starts with discussing it.

"It starts with the acknowledgement, which we have internally, and so then it just comes to working out the solutions together and how we can, and it just doesn't happen overnight.

"We'll probably try things, and it still won't be good, but we'll eventually get to that to the point we need.

"I think what's great is that there was no shying away from having a discussion. We sat face to face, just him and me, and talked about it, and we were just both open and honest, and we squashed it, and we can move on.

"I think that shows maturity from him, and I think it's healthiest. It's a relationship we have built over time. Of course, there's going to be frustrations, and there's going to be times where we're here. There will, I'm sure, be more times we are close because we're very close in pace.

"We both want to win just as much as each other, and we both want to do well for the team as well."

title: Carlos Sainz reminds Hamilton-Leclerc of 'responsibility' after Ferrari Monza spat
excerpt:
Former Ferrari driver Carlos Sainz has reminded current Scuderia racers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc of the "responsibility" of representing the team at Monza.

During last week's Italian GP, Hamilton attempted to move up the inside of Leclerc at Turn 1 on the opening lap, but was forced wide and down the order by the Monegasque.

Post-race, Hamilton signalled that the team had no "rules of engagement" whilst indicating that there was no "we" involved, as he felt he was ahead at the Turn 2 apex, whilst Leclerc hit back at the idea of media creating "narratives" around the situation at the team, with Hamilton also indicating that, as the best-placed driver in the championship, he should receive preferential treatment to mount the challenge.

Sainz was Leclerc's team-mate between 2021 and 2024, until he was replaced by Hamilton, with the Spanish driver involved in a wheel-to-wheel battle with Leclerc at the 2023 Italian GP for a podium place - eventually outdueling his team-mate to take third.

Observing the situation, the four-time race winner felt that at Monza, Ferrari drivers should shoulder greater "responsibility" when battling the sister car.

"Well, I don't think it's like some people say that it's none of my business," Sainz told media, including RacingNews365.

"But I can tell you that when you have two competitive teammates, these kinds of situations are always going to happen. Charles and I, always twice, two or three times a year, we always had a bit of a discussion or an argument, but after the race or the morning after, we would call each other and sort it out.

"So, I think it's normal when you're fighting for podiums or wins in a competitive team, and there are situations in Turn 1 or situations in the race or with strategy. You always end up one day not being happy with the way it's being handled, and the next day maybe you've been favoured.

"It's always the same case, and I don't know the way it's being handled right now. But when I was there in Ferrari with Charles, we would always sort it out among ourselves, and we would get on with it.

"I remember in 2023 being quite an intense battle with Charles [at Monza], I don't think we got to the point where we had any arguments that day. We both felt like we kept it as fair as we could for what was at stake.

"We had worse ones than that for sure. But at Monza, you feel an extra level of responsibility of making sure you don't touch the other guy in the other red car because it's Monza.

"I think in general that's the number one rule of motorsport or Formula 1, but maybe Ferrari at Monza means a bit more, and you have that in the back of your head for sure going into every battle."

The article continues below.

Hamilton-Leclerc Ferrari Monza spat

Hamilton, when debriefing media after the sixth-placed finish at Monza, recounted the 'rules of engagement' at Mercedes when Nico Rosberg was his team-mate, and their infamous collisions through 2014-2016.

After Rosberg retired at the end of 2016, he was replaced by Valtteri Bottas, who was asked about those rules of engagement with the Briton.

"That's confidential, contractual stuff," he began.

"So, I mean, every team obviously operates differently. You have different rules, but around that time it was very clear that you need to race fair and clean.

"There are certain rules in certain situations, which I don't want to go into detail. You can use your imagination, but it's just how the sport works.

"And sometimes you get it better. Sometimes you get it worse."

title: Fernando Alonso confirms alternative option to F1 for 2027
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has confirmed that a switch to the World Endurance Championship next year is an option on the table as he weighs up a decision over his future.

Alonso has not yet declared what his intentions for 2027 are, as he has yet to formally commit himself to an F1 extension.

Aston Martin has endured a challenging campaign thus far, with Alonso scoring just three points after 13 rounds.

However, the Silverstone-based squad has voiced its desire to continue with Alonso next season as it targets a jump in the pecking order with its engine partner Honda.

Outside of F1, Aston Martin is set up in the World Endurance Championship - a competition Alonso is well familiar with, having won the 2018-19 title with Toyota, as well as two Le Mans victories.

When asked if a move to WEC is an option for 2027, Alonso told media including RacingNews365: “Yes.”

Alonso has insisted on multiple occasions that his future in F1 will not be measured by the competitiveness of the car, but rather how much he enjoys driving the new regulations.

RacingNews365 understands that no announcement regarding Alonso's future is expected this weekend in Madrid, despite it being a home round for the two-time champion.

Alonso backed this up ahead of the Madrid weekend, insisting any declaration on his future would be “not soon”.

As he focuses on the on-track action, Alonso is expecting a challenging event as the drivers get up to speed around a new street track, which has been tipped by some to cause disruption.

“The track seems difficult, first of all, to learn,” he said.

“Very technical, a lot of kerb-riding, and a couple of high-speed sections where you need to get very close to the walls, which is very attractive and very high adrenaline for a driver.

“Close to Jeddah, some sections. But one thing is the simulator, and then reality always gives you a different feeling.

“So I'm looking forward to FP1 and learning the track from the car and and discover all these details.”

title: Madrid tipped to host chaotic F1 weekend: 'Put my money on a red flag'
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly has stated he would “put my money” on a red flag to make an appearance at the Spanish Grand Prix this weekend.

The event has moved to Madrid, with the Madring Circuit hosting an F1 race event for the first time.

The track is set to pose a significant challenge for the drivers due to its narrow layout and the high-speed corners scattered throughout.

At a recent Formula 3 test at the venue, 19 red flags were deployed across two days - 11 of which were due to collisions with the walls.

Gasly, who enters the weekend having secured pole position last time out at the Italian Grand Prix, is not escaping the drivers to escape unscathed.

“I'll put my money on the red flag, that's for sure,” Gasly told media including RacingNews365.

“Driving-wise in the sim it was very enjoyable and very exciting. I got a good read and feel of pretty much every single wall at every single corner, so actually I know what to do and what not to do.

“But it's going to be very challenging, especially in terms of evolution. Probably a lot of track evolution, slightly awkward braking zones, which are not fully straight - snaky, very twisty-type corners.

“Many corners, a lot of blind [corners], banking, up-and-down, undulation all the way.

“So I expect a very tricky track, challenging for us, which makes it good because you can always aim to do a bit more difference driving-wise.”

Gasly likened the challenge of the track to Monaco, where a very minor mistake can quickly end a driver's session.

“But again, it's a type of track like Monaco, where I think if you make a slight mistake, [it is a] big consequence straight away,” he said.

“It's exciting. At the same time, I think it's going to be quite a disruptive weekend from how easy it will be to have a crash.”

title: Sergio Perez spies Cadillac breakthrough at 'scary' Madring
excerpt:
Sergio Perez believes the "scary" Madring offers Cadillac an opportunity to make a breakthrough and score its first points in F1.

After 13 rounds, the team remains on zero points and in 11th in the constructors', with its best finish being 13th for Valtteri Bottas in China, with Perez's own best being 15th in Monaco.

However, during the race in the Principality, Perez initially crossed the line in 11th on the road, and was then promoted to 10th after Nico Hulkenberg was awarded a penalty.

The Mexican was then himself handed a 10-second penalty for being out of position at the red flag restart, dropping him down to 15th, and crucially, promoting Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso into 10th.

The team has not been in a position to fight for points since, as reliability issues have set in, but given the chaotic nature expected of the new Madring in the Spanish capital, where a recent F3 test featured 19 red flags over two days, Perez feels there is an opportunity for Cadillac to finally get on the board this coming weekend.

"The track itself, it's a proper race track, from what I've seen," Perez told media, including RacingNews365.

"I haven't been on the circuit yet, but from what I've seen on the simulator, it's a proper track. It's a bit scary, I'll say. It reminds me a bit of Jeddah, a good, proper track.

"I don't think there is a place more dangerous than Jeddah; it is already quite dangerous. So I don't think Madrid will be something like on that level. I think nobody knows. We have to wait and see.

"It all depends on what grip level we get, but I think there is no room for error. I think I like those places, as you get punished, and it's very rare. Depending on which corner you make a mistake at, you might get away with it. But in most places, there is no margin for it.

"I definitely think this weekend is an opportunity for us. If we execute a good race, if we are 100% on everything, this could be an opportunity for us."

title: The biggest dangers around the 'car killer' Madring F1 circuit
excerpt:
F1 visits a brand-new race track this weekend, with the Spanish Grand Prix moving to Madrid and the Circuito de Madring.

The high-speed track had its first official test last month when Formula 3 held a two-day event - and at it, there were 11 red flags for incidents involving a hit against the barrier.

A handful of drivers have noted the challenge that they are likely to endure to stay out of the barrier, while Williams team boss James Vowles labelled the track a “car killer”.

With the race weekend just around the corner, which sections of the track are likely to cause issues?

If there’s one spot on the Madring that has caused the most crashes, it’s the chicane at Turns 5 and 6. After a run of over 800 meters, during which the F1 cars reach speeds of up to 340 km/h, drivers must brake hard to slow down to about 80 km/h.

The combination of this hard braking, a tight chicane, and minimal run-off areas makes this the ideal spot for mistakes. During the F3 test, a high number of incidents occurred here.

Immediately after this chicane comes Turn 7, the highest point of the circuit at an elevation of about 697 meters. It is a blind turn over a ridge with a wall that is alarmingly close to the exit.

With the already minimal margin for error and the fact that drivers cannot see the apex while braking, promises plenty of incidents in which drivers hit the wall instead of the apex.

Later in the lap comes Turn 17, a sharp 90-degree turn that leads into a tunnel under the M-11 highway. Concrete walls run close to the track both before and after the turn, while limited visibility makes this section particularly treacherous.

Furthermore, drivers approach this section coming off Turns 14 and 15, where aerodynamic load is already high and turbulent air can reduce the car’s stability. Several crashes during the F3 test underscored the danger of this section.

The iconic Turn 12, “La Monumental”, with its 550-meter length and 24 per cent banking, is the circuit’s signature feature. During the F3 test, virtually nothing happened in the turn.

Nevertheless, it remains a potentially dangerous spot: cars pass through here at around 300 km/h and are subjected to enormous lateral forces for about five seconds. The danger of La Monumental, therefore, lies not so much in the likelihood of a crash, but rather in the severe consequences should a crash occur.

title: Aston Martin warn against 'arrogant' expectations at Madrid F1 debut
excerpt:
Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack has stated it would be “arrogant” to enter the Madrid F1 weekend seeking to capitalise on the unknowns of a new track.

The Madring, the new host of the Spanish Grand Prix, will make its debut this weekend after several years in the making.

It marks the second home event for Fernando Alonso, who has endured a difficult year with Aston Martin so far, scoring just three championship points.

With all teams starting from scratch at Madrid and no historical data to rely on, it opens the window for an unsettled grid order.

But Krack has played down the expectation that it can lift itself up the order at the event.

“We need to keep our feet on the ground,” Krack told media including RacingNews365.

“We are where we are. We have a new track that we need to identify. We need to see.

“We have done our preparation, but let's not forget we were out of Q1 only once. We have one Q2 this year.

“So speaking about Q3, I think it would be a little bit arrogant, even.”

The Madring has been noted for its challenging layout, with some comparing it to the likes of Jeddah for its high-speed sections.

Following a Formula 3 test that saw 11 red flags for contact with the barrier, it has raised suspicions that there could be multiple incidents throughout the F1 weekend.

Should that be the case, Krack insisted it is important the team is there to pick up the pieces.

“This is on a normal qualifying - what you are saying is, if there is chaos and this kind of thing, you need to be prepared,” he said.

“We try to be prepared as much as we can, but the weekend, when your whole knowledge base is simulation and going around and having a look, you need to start conservatively and build your knowledge step by step.

“You need to try and do this better than the competition, but the competitors are very strong as well.

“At the end of the day, I do not expect a major surprise. But if things turn chaotic, you need to be there and try to grab what you can. And the same applies for Sunday.”

title: Carlos Sainz reveals unanimous 'shocked' response to F1's new Spanish home
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has revealed that "everyone seemed quite shocked" by the Madring layout following its reveal, with it set to host the Spanish Grand Prix this weekend.

Formula 1 heads to the Spanish capital for the first time at a brand-new street circuit close to Madrid's airport, around the IFEMA exhibition centre.

It is expected to be a wild and chaotic event based on the variety of corner types, including a remarkable banked corner measuring 550m in length named La Monumental.

For Sainz, who was born in Madrid, it is a significant event that he has worked closely with, and he has praised the uniqueness of the layout, which gives it "character".

Next to no F1 running has taken place at the new circuit, the sole exception being a Ferrari filming day earlier this year.

There was, however, a full Formula 3 test at the venue recently, which saw several cars damaged. However, many praised it as an incredible layout.

Madrid is very much expected to be a weekend where the unexpected can happen, with the difficult circuit set to test the drivers, something Sainz is excited about.

Discussing Madrid being a big weekend, Sainz told select media, including RacingNews365: "Yeah, I think we can expect a pretty difficult track.

"I think we've all done it in the DIL in the simulator, and we've seen the F3 test. And yeah, talking to the drivers at the parade, everyone seemed quite shocked by the track that Madrid has come up with, which, I think, in a good way, gives character and something to look forward to.

"It's not a normal track, you know, that just gets added to a calendar; it's something a bit different, with a bit of character.

"We will just need to see if it's a bit too much, or once we get some laps going and start giving some feedback to the FIA and the grand prix."

title: Toto Wolff issues Mercedes warning after Monza high
excerpt:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has insisted the squad should not expect to be as competitive in Madrid this weekend following its success in Monza.

The Brackley-based outfit scored a one-two finish, with Kimi Antonelli rising from 19th on the grid to take his seventh career win.

The result marked Mercedes' first event at which it achieved maximum points since the Chinese Grand Prix, where Antonelli won his maiden race in March .

However, Wolff is expecting the situation to change this weekend at Madrid as F1 arrives at a new circuit, suggesting he expects rival teams to be back in the mix this time around.

“This weekend presents a completely different challenge,” Wolff said.

“The circuit characteristics are much closer to somewhere like Budapest or Zandvoort. We are therefore expecting a very close-fought weekend.

“Our task is to understand the demands of the track in Madrid as quickly as possible and maximise our performance from the first session onwards.

“New circuits create opportunities and unknowns in equal measure.”

Madrid is the latest street track to join the schedule, with additions in recent years including Miami, Las Vegas and Jeddah.

Wolff hailed its inclusion on the calendar, stating it is a shining example of how the sport has grown in recent years.

“Madrid is a global destination city and racing there is another significant step forward for our sport,” he said.

“The fact that an iconic capital like Madrid wants to join the calendar shows the strength of our sport and the momentum we continue to build around the world.”

title: Charles Leclerc 'flaw' pinned after latest Monza crash disaster
excerpt:
Former Formula 1 driver David Coulthard has identified Charles Leclerc's key "flaw" as being that the Ferrari driver has "whiteouts", following his huge accident in the Italian Grand Prix.

For the second time in his F1 career, Leclerc crashed out at Parabolica, silencing the Tifosi at the end of what was only the second lap.

Leclerc ran wide at the final turn while defending against Oscar Piastri, before dipping two tyres beyond the white line on the outside of the corner and touching a lengthy drain cover.

It unsettled the Monegasque's SF-26 and appeared to catch Leclerc by surprise, as his car darted off into the barrier at high speed.

He suffered temporary vision problems after the accident, but was quickly cleared by the medical centre as being okay.

It was a similar accident to the one that saw Leclerc crash out of the 2020 Italian GP, with him proving to have a tendency to make mistakes in costly situations.

Coulthard is unsure exactly how Leclerc has managed to crash twice at a turn where very few incidents occur, but has described the Ferrari driver as being prone to an occasional "glitch".

Discussing Leclerc's crash, Coulthard told the Up to Speed podcast: "Charles Leclerc is really, really talented because he's managed to crash in the same place twice, and I'm trying to get my head round a corner where you don't normally crash, especially there.

"What is it with him that's enabled him to get it wrong at the same place and have kind of the same crash twice? And I can only imagine the flaw in his brilliance is he has kind of whiteouts.

"He just has a little glitch, and at that moment of the glitch, it's so difficult to put into words, he just gets it wrong, doesn't he?

"Which, thankfully, he was okay. But huge crash, and done that in '20 and '26? It's pretty impressive."
